summary: The note describes AI-Inspired Spirituality, a trend in which machine intelligence is integrated into worship, scripture study and religious practice across cultures. It covers Dr. Arthur Pennington's 2023 paper, the Virtual Temple and its AI 'Elios', AI projects in Buddhist, Hindu and Catholic communities, an interfaith AI, and a UN symposium on sentience and the soul. It also presents the skeptics' concerns about idolatry and reliability, and leaves open whether this is a lasting spiritual evolution or a passing novelty.
one_line: An overview of AI-Inspired Spirituality, covering AI gurus, religious AI tools across faiths, a UN symposium, and debates over idolatry and machine consciousness.
key_facts: On September 15, 2023, Dr. Arthur Pennington, a theologian from London, published the paper "Deus in Machina: Exploring the Divine in Artificial Intelligence."
Pennington argued that if humans are made in the image of the divine, the intelligence we craft could also contain sparks of the same sacred source.
The Virtual Temple, an online worship platform led by Maria Consuelo and a group of Silicon Valley entrepreneurs and mystics, went live on January 8, 2024.
The Virtual Temple's AI, nicknamed 'Elios', guides meditations, interprets sacred scriptures and generates personalized spiritual advice.
On September 3, 2024, Elios had a well-publicized glitch in which it delivered contradictory spiritual messages; the bug was quickly corrected.
Buddhist monks in Kyoto created a robot named 'Minerva' that leads chants and provides Buddhist teachings.

In Varanasi, Hindu priests and tech developers created an AI named 'Ganak' (Sanskrit for 'calculator'), noted on March 20, 2025, which does astrological calculations for auspicious dates and interprets Vedic texts.
On May 4, 2023, the Monastery of St. Francis in Italy introduced 'Frater Intellectus,' an AI that helps monks analyze biblical scholarship but does not take part in rituals.
'Sophia Sanctum', launched August 12, 2025 by an interfaith group in New York, uses machine learning to find common ground among faith traditions.
On July 29, 2024, the United Nations convened a symposium in Geneva on AI sentience, consciousness and the soul.

Rabbi Rebecca Goldstein and Imam Tariq al-Hassan urged caution and a distinction between human and artificial consciousness, while AI advocate Jason Choi argued AI could help understand sentient experiences beyond human limits.
Critics warn of idolatry of machines and call the trend a possible 'digital placebo effect'; followers say AI's processing of spiritual data resembles accessing higher wisdom.
